prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer sits looking down at a narrow manicure table about 0.4–0.6 metres away, with another person seated opposite across the table at roughly 0.5–0.8 metres and the tiled floor receding behind the table to about 1.2–1.5 metres. Brightest in the foreground (0.3–0.4 metres) are the camera wearer's two arms extending from the bottom edge, holding the other person's extended right hand (at ~0.45 metres) in the left hand while moving a pink nail file with the right hand, with both people's legs partially visible beneath the table at 0.6–0.9 metres. Across the table, the other person's torso (partially cropped at the top edge, so their head and gaze direction are out of view) faces toward the camera wearer, with their left hand resting near a tape roll and scissors on the right side of the table while bottles and jars sit on the left, all within 0.3–0.6 metres and within arm's reach of both people. Across the five frames, the depth values remain largely static except for the camera wearer's right hand and nail file tilting and shifting back and forth by a few centimetres around the fingertips of the opposite person's right hand, partially occluding the fingers and table edge. The map clarifies the vertical layering between the raised hands, the tabletop, the upright bottle on the left, and the recessed legs and floor below, though it looks unreliable along the bottom-left edge of every frame where a bright vertical streak falsely indicates a near surface over the floor and chair.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map divides the foreground into two distinct `person` masks—one for the camera wearer's lower arms and legs at the bottom (0.3–0.7 metres away) and one for the opposite person's upper torso and arms at the top (0.45–0.8 metres away), who faces the camera wearer with their head cropped out of the top of the frame. Between and beneath their meeting hands lies a `dining table` mask representing the manicure table at 0.4–0.6 metres, with a small `cup` mask identifying a round white jar on the left side of the table (~0.5 metres from the camera wearer and ~0.2 metres left of the hands), all within arm's reach of both individuals. The masks clearly trace the contact boundary and mutual occlusion where the camera wearer's left fingers and the nail file overlap the opposite person's right fingertips in the centre of the frame, while across the five frames the camera wearer's right-hand mask pivots from angled right (frame 1) to horizontal (frames 2–3) and back to angled right (frames 4–5). This map makes the exact pixel boundaries separating the two entangled sets of hands and forearms easier to distinguish than in the RGB strip alone. However, it is unreliable in frame 2 where the `dining table` mask disappears completely, in frame 4 where the tape dispenser on the right is misclassified as a `cup`, in frame 5 where the two people's masks merge and swap colours across thecamera wearer's wrists, and throughout the strip where the right half of the table and most tabletop tools (bottles, scissors, nail file, phone) go unsegmented.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders only 2D hand skeletons in magenta on a black background, showing no yellow body skeletons because both the camera wearer's torso and the opposite person's head and shoulders are out of view at the bottom and top edges of the frame. In the centre of the scene (roughly 0.35–0.5 metres from the camera wearer), three hands are tracked within immediate reach and contact of one another: the opposite person's right hand extending downward from the top-left with fingers spread toward the camera wearer, the camera wearer's left hand reaching up from the bottom-left to support those fingertips, and the camera wearer's right hand reaching from the bottom-right holding the nail file. Across the five frames, the opposite person's right hand stays stationary while the camera wearer's right-hand skeleton rotates inward in frames 2 and 3 to bring the file horizontally across the middle finger before pivoting back to the right in frames 4 and 5. Compared to the RGB image, the wireframe joints make the exact finger flexion, pinch posture, and spatial overlap of the three interacting hands immediately apparent despite heavy occlusion from the nail file and overlapping digits. However, the map is unreliable where it completely misses the camera wearer's left-hand skeleton in frames 3 and 5, fails to detect the opposite person's resting left hand in the upper-right quadrant (~0.6 metres away) across all five frames, and collapses the camera wearer's right-hand finger joints into a tangled cluster during the close overlap in frame 3.
